```{r discussion-setup, include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)

# Resolve the project root
.find_root <- function(start = getwd()) {
  path <- normalizePath(start, winslash = "/")
  while (!file.exists(file.path(path, "_quarto.yml"))) {
    parent <- normalizePath(dirname(path), winslash = "/")
    if (parent == path) stop("Could not find project root (_quarto.yml)")
    path <- parent
  }
  path
}
.root <- .find_root()
.p <- function(...) file.path(.root, ...)

rep   <- read.csv(.p("results/11_repeatability/repeatability_summary.csv"))
pred  <- read.csv(.p("results/12_predictability/predictability_summary.csv"))
clust <- read.csv(.p("results/14_individual_traits/behaviour_clusters.csv"))

# ── Format helpers ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(round(x, digits), format = "f", digits = digits)

# Repeatability
r_val  <- function(v) fmt(rep$R_cow_mean[rep$variable == v])
r_ci   <- function(v) paste0("[", fmt(rep$R_cow_lower[rep$variable == v]), ", ",
                                   fmt(rep$R_cow_upper[rep$variable == v]), "]")

# CVi
cvi_val <- function(v) fmt(rep$CVi_mean[rep$variable == v])
cvi_ci  <- function(v) paste0("[", fmt(rep$CVi_lower[rep$variable == v]), ", ",
                                    fmt(rep$CVi_upper[rep$variable == v]), "]")

# CVP
cvp_val <- function(v) fmt(pred$CVP_mean[pred$variable == v])
cvp_ci  <- function(v) paste0("[", fmt(pred$CVP_lower[pred$variable == v]), ", ",
                                    fmt(pred$CVP_upper[pred$variable == v]), "]")

# Derived summaries
r_min_var  <- rep$variable[which.min(rep$R_cow_mean)]
r_min_val  <- fmt(min(rep$R_cow_mean))
r_max_var  <- rep$variable[which.max(rep$R_cow_mean)]
r_max_val  <- fmt(max(rep$R_cow_mean))

cvp_min_val <- fmt(min(pred$CVP_mean))
cvp_max_val <- fmt(max(pred$CVP_mean))

cvi_max_var <- rep$variable[which.max(rep$CVi_mean)]
cvi_max_val <- fmt(max(rep$CVi_mean))

c1_vars <- clust$variable[clust$cluster == 1]
n_c1    <- length(c1_vars)

var_labels <- c(
  "feed_intake"                    = "daily feed intake",
  "feed_duration"                  = "daily feeding duration",
  "feed_visits"                    = "daily feeding visits",
  "water_intake"                   = "daily water intake",
  "water_duration"                 = "daily drinking duration",
  "water_visits"                   = "daily drinking visits",
  "total_actor"                    = "daily actor events",
  "total_reactor"                  = "daily reactor events",
  "number_of_non_nutritive_visits" = "daily non-nutritive visits",
  "median_pct_feed_remaining"      = "median proportion of feed remaining at visit start",
  "total_meals"                    = "daily meals",
  "median_meal_duration"           = "median meal duration",
  "median_visit_per_meal"          = "median visits per meal",
  "median_intake_per_meal"         = "median feed intake per meal",
  "median_feeding_pct_per_meal"    = "median percentage of meal time spent feeding",
  "median_non_nutritive_per_meal"  = "median non-nutritive visits per meal"
)

clean_label <- function(v) {
  labels <- var_labels[v]
  ifelse(is.na(labels), gsub("_", " ", v), unname(labels))
}
```

# 4. Discussion

This study demonstrates that existing data streams from electronic feeders and drinkers contain far richer behavioural information than is typically extracted. By developing the `moo4feed` R package, we introduced a standardized and reproducible pipeline for processing raw electronic feeder and drinker data and extracting behavioural variables that go beyond basic daily intake and visit counts. Using 16 variables spanning feeding, drinking, meal patterns, non-nutritive behaviour, and social competition, we quantified repeatability and predictability for each variable, identified behaviours most informative for individual profiling, and used those behaviours to characterize four distinct cow types within the herd.

## 4.1 Repeatability and Predictability in Context

A meta-analysis of 759 repeatability estimates across 114 studies and 98 species reported a mean R of 0.37 [@Bell2009]. Our repeatability values ranged from `r r_min_val` (`r clean_label(r_min_var)`) to `r r_max_val` (`r clean_label(r_max_var)`), with most variables falling between 0.38 and 0.64. This places the majority of our behavioural variables above the cross-species average, indicating that the behaviours captured from electronic feeders and drinkers likely reflect stable individual differences.

Two methodological points are worth noting when comparing our results to previous cattle work. First, none of the previous studies [@thomas2024; @carslake2022b; @occhiuto2022] reported CVi, the coefficient of individual variation. As articulated by Hertel et al. [-@hertel2020], CVi is essential for comparing the magnitude of among-individual differences across studies and populations because R is confounded by within-individual variance: a high R can result from either large among-individual differences or very low day-to-day variability within individuals. Without CVi, it is not possible to determine whether differences in R between studies reflect genuine differences in among-individual variation or merely differences in residual noise. Our study is the first in the cattle repeatability literature to report CVi alongside R, and we encourage future work to adopt this metric to enable meaningful cross-study comparisons. Second, the comparison between our adult cow results and the calf results of Carslake et al. [-@carslake2022b] and Occhiuto et al. [-@occhiuto2022] should be interpreted cautiously. Bell et al. [-@Bell2009] noted that whether juveniles are more or less repeatable than adults of the same species remains an unanswered biological question with no clear directional prediction: juveniles may be less repeatable because they are undergoing rapid developmental change, or more repeatable because the costs of deviating from a developmental trajectory are high. Neave et al. [-@neave2020long] found that bold and exploratory traits were consistent within each rearing period (before and after weaning; after puberty to first lactation), but were not consistent across the pubertal transition, suggesting that major physiological changes at sexual maturation can disrupt previously stable behavioural profiles. The few within-species comparisons available show no consistent pattern. We therefore focus our direct comparisons on Thomas et al. [-@thomas2024], the only other study conducted in adult dairy cows.

For the variables directly comparable to Thomas et al. [-@thomas2024], our estimates are similar or higher. Our R for daily feeding duration (`r r_val("feed_duration")` `r r_ci("feed_duration")`) exceeds their R = 0.38 [0.35, 0.40] for daily feeding time in 2584 adult cows across 46 herds. This difference likely reflects methodological differences rather than a true biological divergence: Thomas et al. used neck-mounted sensors and aggregated data across diverse commercial herds; whereas our study used automated feeders with strict data filtering, removing days affected by illness, lameness, estrus, and other disruptions. These design choices reduce within-individual noise and would be expected to yield higher repeatability estimates. 

Many of our highest-R variables (daily drinking duration: `r r_val("water_duration")`; daily feeding visits: `r r_val("feed_visits")`; daily non-nutritive visits: `r r_val("number_of_non_nutritive_visits")`) capture behaviours that have never been assessed for repeatability before, and have no published comparison. Even our lowest R value (`r clean_label(r_min_var)`: `r r_min_val`) is likely still biologically meaningful. Bell et al. [-@Bell2009] showed that many well-established personality traits in wild populations have R values between 0.20 and 0.40, and Thomas et al. [-@thomas2024] reported their lowest R at 0.21 [0.20, 0.21] for maximum lying bout duration yet interpreted it as evidence of consistent individual differences. For behaviours measured in the broader cattle literature but not in our study (e.g., lying bouts, space use), prior work reports R values ranging from 0.03 to 0.80 in calves and 0.21 to 0.38 in adult cows [@thomas2024; @carslake2022b; @occhiuto2022]. 

For predictability, our CVP values ranged from `r cvp_min_val` to `r cvp_max_val` across all 16 variables. This is notably lower than the cross-species mean CVP of 0.27 [0.22, 0.33] reported across 64 estimates from 39 datasets in a meta-analysis of behavioural and physiological traits [@mitchell2020]. For dairy calves, CVP values in the literature ranged from 0.13 [0.06, 0.21] (total meals; @carslake2022b) to 0.49 [0.35, 0.62] (core area used; @occhiuto2022). For adult dairy cows, Thomas et al. [-@thomas2024] reported CVP values ranging from 0.19 [0.18, 0.20] (daily feeding time) to 0.46 [0.44, 0.48] (mean lying bout duration), with higher values coming from bout-level metrics that are inherently more liabile than daily aggregates. Our corresponding CVP for daily feeding duration was `r cvp_val("feed_duration")` `r cvp_ci("feed_duration")`, which is close to Thomas et al.'s daily feeding time estimate and confirms that our daily-level metrics fall at the lower end of the adult cow range.

The uniformly low CVP values in our study likely reflect the same strict data filtering that inflated our R estimates relative to previous work: by removing days disrupted by illness, lameness, estrus, and regrouping, we restricted our analyses to a stable behavioural baseline. This is a practically useful finding in its own right: under clean baseline conditions, CVP values were consistently low across all variables, and the variation in predictability across cows was modest. Whether individual cow types (e.g., the "fragmented restless feeders" identified in Section 3.3) show systematically higher within-individual variability during periods of health challenge, or whether predictability is better understood as a property of physiological state than of personality, is an important question for future work.

## 4.2 Novel Behavioural Variables and Compensatory Feeding Strategies

A key contribution of this study is showing that electronic feeders capture information well beyond what is typically reported. Standard analyses focus on daily feed and water intake, visit counts, and duration. By applying the `moo4feed` pipeline, we additionally derived variables capturing exploratory behaviour (non-nutritive visits), social competition (actor and reactor replacement events), feeding efficiency (median percentage of meal time spent actively eating), feed access disadvantage (proportion of feed remaining at visit start), and meal fragmentation (median visits per meal). These variables have rarely been considered in the repeatability and predictability literature, which has focused primarily on daily aggregates of feeding and lying behaviours [@thomas2024; @carslake2022b; @occhiuto2022].

Among all variables, non-nutritive visits showed the largest CVi (`r cvi_val("number_of_non_nutritive_visits")` `r cvi_ci("number_of_non_nutritive_visits")`), meaning cows differ from one another by more than half the population mean in how often they visit feed bins without eating. Daily actor events (CVi = `r cvi_val("total_actor")` `r cvi_ci("total_actor")`) and daily reactor events (CVi = `r cvi_val("total_reactor")` `r cvi_ci("total_reactor")`) also showed high among-individual variation. In contrast, daily feed intake (CVi = `r cvi_val("feed_intake")` `r cvi_ci("feed_intake")`) showed the smallest relative variation. The finding that cows are nearly indistinguishable from one another in daily feed intake, despite exhibiting different feeding profiles, suggests compensatory feeding: cows converge to similar intakes through different behavioural pathways. Cow 7068 (frequently replaced, but efficient and sustained feeder) and cow 5042 (fragmented, restless, but fast eater) both achieved high daily feed intakes through opposite strategies. This echoes Thomas et al. [-@thomas2024], who found high repeatability for total daily feeding time and interpreted it as cows compensating disrupted bouts by adjusting other feeding aspects.

## 4.3 Behavioural Profiles and Cow Types

By applying PCA with varimax rotation to the variables with both high R and high CVi, we identified three principal components explaining over 80% of variance. K-means clustering on these component scores identified four cow types: a frequently replaced herd majority, contest-winning cows, water lovers, and fragmented restless feeders.

Personality has been defined as consistent differences in how individual animals respond across contexts and over time [@reale2007]. The four cow types we identified are grounded in variables that showed consistent and large among-individual variation, meaning these cows differed from one another in stable, characteristic ways throughout the observation period. However, we do not claim that this constitutes full personality assessment. Such assessment requires data spanning a longer time window, more diverse contexts, and ideally replication across farms and management systems. However, the patterns we observed are consistent with the personality framework as behavioural differences were not explained purely by the fixed effects in our models. These sensor-derived behavioural profiles appear to reflect some personality-like traits. It is also worth noting that cows in this study were overstocked at the feeder (48 cows for 30 feed bins), which would increase competition for feed access [@sheng2024redefining]. Thus, the behavioural profiles we identified may be a reflection of coping strategies cows developed to access resources under high competition, rather than personality traits [@schwanke2025graduate].

The contrast between "contest-winning" and "frequently-replaced" cows captures persistent differences in competitive success at the feeder, not necessarily dominance. As we noted in previous work [@sheng2024redefining], replacement events are not a clean proxy for dominance: they are often triggered by the motivation to access fresh feed in intensive and competitive environment, rather than by social rank per se. What the cluster analysis captures is not who dominates whom, but who consistently initiates replacements and who consistently yields. Interestingly, some "frequently replaced" cows compensated for this disadvantage through sustained, efficient feeding during the time they did occupy a bin, while "contest-winning" cows, facing fewer disruptions, fed with notably less non-nutritive and exploratory behaviour.

The "water lovers" cluster stands out because these cows spent considerably more time at and returning to the drinkers without drinking more water, suggesting the behaviour is not primarily driven by hydration needs. Cow 7150, whose case we highlighted in detail, showed long drinking durations and frequent drinker visits during a period when THI remained consistently below 68, ruling out heat load as an explanation [@McDonald2020]. The "fragmented, restless feeders" represent a qualitatively distinct type: defined by an exceptionally high rate of non-nutritive visits, these cows approached bins with feed available but withdrew without eating.

## 4.4 Limitations

Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. Data were collected at a single research farm using Holstein dairy cows under specific management conditions, which limits direct generalizability to commercial herds with different pen designs, stocking densities, or feeding management. The dynamic group composition (approximately 6 cows entering and leaving the pen every 16 days) introduced ongoing social instability. 

A methodological strength of our study relative to previous work is the explicit assessment of variable distributions before model fitting. We examined each variable's distribution and selected Gaussian or lognormal likelihoods accordingly (Section 2.4). The choice of likelihood family matters because it affects the scale on which variance components are estimated and therefore the resulting R and CVi values.

For the total meals variable, we used a lognormal model (log transformation) because the raw distribution was strongly right-skewed. Although total meals is technically a count variable and could in principle be modeled with a negative binomial distribution, we chose the lognormal approach for two reasons. First, the primary goal was to compare repeatability and predictability across all 16 variables on a common scale. Using a different distributional family for one variable would have required simulation-based methods to extract comparable R and CVi estimates, making direct comparison across variables much more complex. Second, the same issue applies to feeding rate and drinking rate, which we excluded from the current analysis entirely because their distributions could not be adequately normalized even after log transformation. Fitting these variables with appropriate non-Gaussian families and deriving comparable repeatability metrics through simulation is beyond the scope of this paper but represents a worthwhile extension for future work.

## 4.5 Future Directions

Several new directions could be explored based on this work. First, the `moo4feed` R package should be applied to other species and study systems (e.g., goats, birds) to evaluate whether the behavioural extraction pipeline and the analytical framework is generalizable beyond dairy cattle. The package was designed with flexibility in mind, and testing its applicability across diverse farm settings would strengthen its utility as a general tool for behavioural phenotyping.

Second, future research should explore the temporal and spatial dimensions of feeding behaviour. Our analyses characterized what cows do on average across the day, but not when or where they choose to compete for access to food and water. During feed delivery, we observed that certain "popular" bins received fresh feed first and attracted disproportionately high competition, even though fresh feed was delivered to all bins. Cows likely differ in their temporal strategies: some may head straight to the most popular bins during peak competition times (arguably a risky, costly approach), while others may access fresh feed at the same high-competition time but choose less popular bins that still have fresh feed yet are more isolated from herd traffic. Understanding whether individual cows consistently adopt one temporal strategy over another would add a new dimension to behavioural profiling.

Third, future work should investigate social relationships between specific cows. Are there stable bonds within the herd, pairs that always feed together or next to each other? Are there strong antagonisms where particular individuals always replace each other? Understanding these dyadic patterns could enhanve our understanding about the social network structure of farm animals.

Fourth, changes in these behaviours over time, and especially changes in a cow's predictability (a highly consistent cow suddenly showing large variation in her behaviour), could serve as early indicators of disease or distress. The personality-dependent sickness behaviour documented by Setser et al. [-@setser2024a] in calves, where fearful and active calves changed their lying behaviour in opposite directions when sick, suggests that the four cow types identified here may respond to illness differently. Prospective validation of whether individual behavioural profiles predict the nature, direction, and timing of health-related behavioural changes would be the critical translational step toward individualized health monitoring.

Finally, while the `moo4feed` package currently takes in data from electronic feeders and drinkers, it was designed in a modular and flexible way. If computer vision systems or other technologies become available that can record which cow eats where and when, the package can accommodate these alternative data sources as long as they output the same fundamental information: individual identity, location, timing, and intake.
